analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the FCC's power to cap and reduce cable TV rates.
analysis.headline: The bill to keep FCC cable rate regulation from expiring in March 1999 never got a hearing or a vote, and the price protections lapsed on schedule.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the 1996 telecom law, the Federal Communications Commission had the power to review cable programming rates and cut them when it found they were unreasonable. That power was set to expire on March 31, 1999. This bill deleted the expiration date, making rate regulation permanent so the FCC could keep policing cable prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who would keep an independent regulator empowered to challenge and reduce cable programming rates after March 1999 instead of facing whatever rates operators chose to charge.

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently extends the FCC's authority to determine whether cable programming rates are reasonable and, in appropriate cases, to reduce them.
It does this by striking the provision that terminates that authority on March 31, 1999, eliminating the sunset written into the 1996 telecom law's rate rules.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, whose freedom to set programming rates would be permanently constrained and whose revenues could be reduced if the FCC ordered rate cuts; any such constraints could also limit the money operators put into network upgrades and new programming.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation limits the revenue cable operators can earn, which operators argued leaves less money for network upgrades, new channels, and service improvements.

A regulator judging 'reasonable' rates can make mistakes or freeze prices below levels that support investment, and by the late 1990s satellite TV was emerging as a competitor, giving critics an argument that market forces rather than price caps should discipline cable rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to see: it keeps a regulator with the power to force cable rate cuts in place indefinitely, at a time when cable bills were rising. The cost is real but harder to measure: operators lose pricing freedom, and in a bad case regulation could slow investment in cable infrastructure. Whether that trade-off favors consumers depends on how much competition satellite providers actually provided in local markets, which varied widely.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the Cable Consumer Protection Act of 1998 on February 25, 1998, with 25 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On March 3, 1998, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
The FCC's cable rate authority was set to terminate on March 31, 1999, so the expiration the bill sought to prevent took effect without Congress acting.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators came out ahead: the March 31, 1999 expiration took effect as written, freeing them from federal rate regulation without this bill or any successor ever reaching a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable operators, freed from rate caps

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make FCC cable rate regulation permanent.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chairman and subcommittee leadership of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee on March 3, 1998, and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cable television industry
against.role: Cable operators facing the loss of rate-setting freedom
against.what_they_did: Opposed extension of federal cable rate regulation, arguing rates should be set by competition rather than the FCC.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so the only partisan signal is sponsorship: 22 of 25 cosponsors were Democrats and 3 were Republicans, while the committee that let the bill die was controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently allowed the FCC to find cable programming rates unreasonable and order reductions, capping operators' pricing power. Its failure let that authority expire in March 1999, leaving subscribers facing whatever rates operators set.
